topic.title: How a Chip Factory Prints Billions of Switches With Light

title: How Does ASML's EUV Machine Print a Chip With Light?
description:
How does a machine print the chip in your phone with light, line by line, finer than anything a lens can focus?
We follow the light through ASML's EUV machine in 3D: molten tin drops hit twice by a laser, a glowing plasma, a row of mirrors in a vacuum, a patterned mask, and the silicon wafer below it.
Then the newest High-NA machine that prints even finer lines, and how the switches of a chip are built up, layer after layer.

0:00 A machine that blasts tin
0:35 The tin drop
1:22 Two laser hits
2:31 Mirrors, not lenses
3:17 The mask
4:02 The wafer
4:57 High-NA: even finer
5:29 Layer after layer
6:23 Back to your phone

Sources: ASML (Nov 2026).
Animations are simplified illustrations, not exact to scale.

lines.text: The chip in a modern phone holds billions of tiny switches, and its finest lines were printed with light made by blowing up drops of molten tin.
The machine that does it, built by ASML, is about the size of a bus, and it blasts 50,000 drops of tin every second. So how does exploding metal end up as a chip?
Follow the light through it. Tin becomes light, mirrors carry it, a mask gives it a pattern, and a silicon wafer takes the print.
Along the way, we'll see why no lens can do this job, how the newest machine prints even finer, and how one print becomes a working switch.
It starts with tin, a soft silvery metal, heated until it melts and flows like water.
A nozzle squeezes it out as a stream of tiny drops, each about 25 microns across, narrower than a human hair.
Each one leaves the nozzle at about 70 metres a second, and they never stop coming.
That's faster than a car on a motorway, and the nozzle aims every one of them at the same tiny spot.
How many? 50,000 drops every second, falling one after another through the very same spot.
Why so many? Because every drop will become one short flash of light, and the machine needs a nonstop stream of flashes.
And it all happens in a vacuum. This kind of light is swallowed by almost everything, even the air.
But a drop of tin doesn't glow on its own. So what turns it into light?
A laser. As each drop falls, a first, weaker pulse hits it and squashes it flat, like a tiny pancake.
Why flatten it? A wide, flat target catches far more of the next pulse, the big one.
That main pulse is far more powerful, and it hits the pancake so hard that the tin becomes plasma, a gas so hot its atoms lose some of their electrons.
And that plasma glows. Not with light you could see, but with extreme ultraviolet light, at a wavelength of 13.5 nanometres.
What does that mean? The light our eyes see has waves many times longer. A shorter wave draws a finer line, like a sharp pencil next to a thick marker.
Then it all repeats. Drop, flatten, flash, 50,000 times a second.
Behind every flash, a big curved mirror gathers the light and focuses it to one bright point at the far end of the chamber.
Why tin, of all things? Tin plasma happens to glow brightly at just this wavelength, so more of each flash is light the machine can use.
So far: a drop, a flash, and light at 13.5 nanometres. Now it has to cross the machine, and this is where ordinary optics fail.
Why not a lens? A camera or a microscope bends light through glass. Try that here, and the glass simply swallows it.
So the light's path has no lenses at all. The machine steers it with mirrors instead.
Not ordinary mirrors, though. Each one is made of many very thin layers, two materials stacked one on top of the other.
Each layer reflects back a little of the light, and all those small reflections line up into one strong bounce.
Why does that matter? Even the best mirror loses part of the light on every bounce, and the light bounces many times on its way down.
It is the reason the source must be so bright, and why these mirrors are polished to some of the smoothest surfaces ever made.
So the light arrives clean and bright. But it carries no picture yet. Where does the pattern of a chip come from?
From the mask: a plate carrying the pattern of one layer of the chip, like a stencil.
And even the mask is a mirror. The light bounces off its pattern instead of shining through it.
Dark parts of it swallow the light, bright parts bounce it back, so the bounce carries the shape of the pattern.
That's also why the mask must stay perfectly clean. A single speck of dust on it would be printed onto every chip, again and again.
And each of the chip's finest layers gets its own mask. Swap the mask, and the same machine prints a different layer.
Then more mirrors shrink that picture down and aim it at the wafer below, far smaller than the mask itself.
Drawing the mask bigger than the print it makes keeps its pattern easier to make accurately.
And what is all that light printing onto?
A wafer: a thin, polished disc of silicon, coated with a film called a resist, which changes wherever the light lands.
It sits on a stage that races back and forth under the light, printing the pattern again and again, chip after chip, across the whole disc.
When one chip is done, the stage jumps to the next spot, and the next sweep begins, until every spot on the disc is printed.
Above it, the mask moves too, in perfect step, so every line lands exactly where it should.
How does the light print a whole chip at once? It doesn't. A thin slit of light sweeps across each one, like a scanner copying a page.
When the disc is done, it holds rows of identical chips, every one a copy of the same layer.
And the finest lines a standard EUV machine prints are about 13 nanometres wide.
So far: tin becomes light, mirrors carry it, the mask shapes it, and the wafer takes the print. And the newest machine goes further.
It's called High-NA. Its mirrors are much bigger, and they catch the light at wider angles.
Why does a wider angle help? Light arriving from more directions can be focused to a tighter point, and a tighter point draws a finer line.
The result: lines about 8 nanometres wide, where the standard machine draws 13.
That's lines about 1.6× finer, so more switches fit on the same patch of silicon.
Yet one pass under this light never makes a chip. A single pass prints just one layer, and a chip needs dozens of them.
What happens after the print? The wafer leaves the machine, and the resist is washed away where the light changed it, leaving a stencil.
Then the gaps in that stencil are etched into the surface, or filled with metal.
The leftover resist is stripped off, a fresh layer goes on top, and the wafer goes back for the next print.
Print, wash, etch, fill: the same loop runs again for every layer, each one lined up exactly on the one below.
At the very bottom, the first layers build the switches themselves: transistors, each a tiny gate that lets current through or blocks it.
What joins them up? Above them, layer after layer of copper wiring connects billions of those switches together.
And not every layer needs EUV. The bigger, coarser layers go to older machines that use longer-wave light, which costs less.
Only the finest layers, the ones packed tightest, take the trip through the tin and the mirrors.
After weeks of this, the finished wafer is sliced into separate chips.
One of them is packaged, tested, and soldered onto the board inside a phone like yours.
So follow that chip back one last time. Its switches were printed by light, the light was steered by mirrors, and the mirrors were lit by a flash.
The most advanced chips in phones, laptops and data centres all depend on a machine like this one.
A flash from one drop of tin, flattened, then blasted by a laser, one of 50,000 every second.
All so the phone in your hand can carry billions of switches on a chip smaller than a fingernail.
What should we open up next? Tell us. Somewhere right now, another drop of tin is about to become light.
